extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners; patent attorneys/agents; patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103: how to assess the level of ordinary skill in the art, establish a prima facie case, articulate rationales for combining references, avoid hindsight, and weigh applicant rebuttal and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be considered in determining the level of ordinary skill in the art may include: (A) “type of problems encountered in the art;” (B) “prior art solutions to those problems;” (C) “rapidity with which innovations are made;” (D) “sophistication of the technology; and” (E) “educational level of active workers in the field.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case may not present every factor and one or more factors may predominate. See In re GPAC and cited cases for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of problems encountered in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: "type of problems encountered in the art" (one enumerated factor used to determine level of ordinary skill)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the technical challenges practitioners faced at the relevant time; used together with other factors to define the hypothetical skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art solutions to those problems
rubrics_metrics.description: "prior art solutions to those problems" (one enumerated factor used to determine level of ordinary skill)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine what prior art taught as solutions — both successful and unsuccessful approaches inform the skilled person's knowledge and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapidity with which innovations are made
rubrics_metrics.description: "rapidity with which innovations are made" (one enumerated factor used to determine level of ordinary skill)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields with rapid innovation may have a higher baseline of ordinary skill and familiarity with recent techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication of the technology
rubrics_metrics.description: "sophistication of the technology" (one enumerated factor used to determine level of ordinary skill)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More sophisticated technical fields may imply a higher level of training/skill for the hypothetical person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational level of active workers in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: "educational level of active workers in the field" (one enumerated factor used to determine level of ordinary skill)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider typical education/training of practitioners (e.g., technicians vs. Ph.D. researchers) as evidence of the skilled person's abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical person of ordinary skill: ordinary creativity and inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person of ordinary skill in the art is also a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton." (KSR). Office personnel may take into account "the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill in the art would employ."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The skilled person can fit teachings of multiple patents together and can perform ordinary inventive steps and inferences; examiners should account for such creativity when reasoning about obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification disclosure as evidence of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of disclosure in the specification of the application or in relevant references may be informative of the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill in the art; silence in the specification on how to achieve a step may suggest that achieving it is within ordinary skill, provided the specification complies with 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the application specification and cited references as circumstantial evidence of what a skilled person would know or be able to do (see Uber Techs. v. X One example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-prior-art references to demonstrate level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: References which are not prior art may be relied upon to demonstrate the level of ordinary skill in the art at or around the relevant time (e.g., contemporaneous invention evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous internal documents or near-simultaneous inventions can be probative of the knowledge in the art and may show motivation to combine even if not prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: If prior art itself reflects appropriate level, specifying level not necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record pertaining to the level of skill in the art are found within the prior art of record, a specific finding of a particular level of skill may be unnecessary where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the prior art clearly demonstrates the skills and knowledge baseline, the examiner need not make a separate detailed factual finding about the skilled person (see Chore‑Time Equip. v. Cumberland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain level of ordinary skill to maintain objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The importance of resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art lies in the necessity of maintaining objectivity in the obviousness inquiry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine obviousness from the viewpoint of the person of ordinary skill, not from viewpoint of the inventor, a judge, layman, remote-arts practitioners, or geniuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness framework and burden allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination and reexamination, the examiner must first set forth a prima facie case, supported by evidence, showing why the claims would have been obvious in light of the prior art. Once the examiner sets out this prima facie case, the burden shifts to the patentee to provide evidence or argument sufficient to rebut the examiner's evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner fails to establish a prima facie case, applicant has no obligation to rebut. If prima facie case is established, applicant may submit evidence (e.g., comparative test data) or arguments; examiner must then weigh all evidence in making the final determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight and correct temporal perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach a proper determination under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner must step backward in time and into the shoes worn by the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art — that time is "before the effective filing date of the claimed invention" (or at time of invention for pre-AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of the applicant's disclosure must be put aside to avoid hindsight, though it can inform differences and searches; explicit factual basis from prior art must support the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action requirements for a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon; (B) the difference(s) in the claim over the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferably cite relevant column/page/line numbers for references. Include every reference relied on, even if minor, so the record clearly communicates basis for rejection (see In re Hoch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for explicit reasoning and factual underpinning
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness (KSR; In re Kahn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit factual findings that link to the legal conclusion; apply the flexible KSR approach but ensure factual support is on the record. Absent articulated rationale, labels such as 'common sense' are insufficient (In re Van Os; Ball Aerosol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of the evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate determination of patentability is based on the entire record, by a preponderance of evidence, with due consideration to the persuasiveness of any arguments and any evidence properly made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner's evidence of obviousness must, as a whole, be more convincing than opposing evidence. Rebuttal evidence submitted by applicant must be evaluated along with the facts supporting obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is a rationale that may support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the KSR-consistent rationales; must be accompanied by appropriate factual findings (see separate required-finding checklist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results is a rationale supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the substituted element was known and that the substitution yields predictable results to a skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way is a rationale supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the technique was known in the art and that its application to the claimed device would have been an ordinary design choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results is a rationale supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the device was amenable to the technique and that the improvement would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try" – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success, may be a rationale supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this rationale only where solutions were finite/predictable and a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success (not where experimentation was extensive/unpredictable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show predictability across fields and that the variation would have been an expected adaptation by a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art (rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While explicit teaching of motivation is not always required, examiners should articulate inferences or routine steps that would provide motivation to combine; link factual findings to the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required factual findings for combination-by-known-methods rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the 'combining prior art elements according to known methods' rationale, Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art included each element claimed (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and that each element performs same function as it does separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness rejection. Use factual record to justify each finding; see Anderson's-Black Rock and KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away reduces likelihood of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prior art criticizes, discredits, or otherwise discourages the solution claimed (teaches away), that prior art weighs against a finding of obviousness; mere disclosure of alternatives alone does not constitute teaching away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art suggests the combination would be impractical or undesirable, demonstrate why a skilled artisan would nonetheless have adopted it; cases like Adams and Crocs illustrate how teaching away supports nonobviousness.
